To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
increased likelihood of a target, compared with low target likelihood, enhances delta oscillations and that delta phase modulates detection rates for probable target events.
high stimulus probability increases delta phase reset and that this effect is stronger than the effect of high stimulus probability on the amplitude of delta oscillations.
the phase of ongoing low-frequency brain oscillations is reset by a stimulus when the stimulus is expected, but the stimulus is not expected when the phase is in a different phase.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of how the brain can use a temporal cue to select a target from a large number of incoming sensory inputs.
the question of how the brain processes information in a situation where temporal cues are not fully predictable.
the question how the brain deals with temporal uncertainties.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
top-down effects of stimulus expectation are not limited to the case of highly predictable timing.
top-down processes are engaged in the delta band to facilitate processing of probable events when temporal uncertainty is restricted within a limited time frame.
the brain uses a mixture of bottom-up and top-down processes to facilitate processing of predictable events.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
top–down processes, such as stimulus expectancy, can be used to align incoming information to high excitability phases of oscillations, even when the timing of the information is not predictable.
top–down effects of stimulus expectancy can be observed even in a situation of mixed uncertainty and that this can be explained by phase-reset effects of low-frequency oscillations.
top–down effects are engaged to facilitate the processing of predictable events, even when the exact timing of such events is not known.
The main takeaway from our work is that
top–down attention can be used to align incoming information to ongoing oscillations even if the timing of the information is uncertain.

the brain can exploit the temporal uncertainty of a cue to enhance the temporal resolution of the sensory input by increasing the phase of ongoing low-frequency activity at the time of the expected event.
top–down effects can be elicited even when the exact timing of the target is unpredictable.
